# Needs assessment (DeepSeek)

<!-- Generated by DeepSeek (chat.deepseek.com, default model, "Thought for 48 seconds") from prompt_pack.md on 13 Oct 2026; final answer copied verbatim from the chat. Section headings re-marked as Markdown headings; MCQ options joined on one line per question. -->

## Background and burden

Glioma is the most common primary brain tumor and is often associated with treatment resistance and poor prognosis [PMID:37458855]. Standard treatment typically involves radiotherapy and temozolomide-based chemotherapy, both of which induce cellular senescence as a tumor suppression mechanism [PMID:37458855]. Glioblastomas routinely treated with ionizing radiation inevitably recur and develop therapy resistance [PMID:34580063]. Recurrent glioblastoma is clinically challenging with 10-15 months overall survival [PMID:39021199]. Glioblastoma has a median survival of only 15 months [PMID:34825085]. Residual disease after chemo-/radiotherapy is linked to senescence and rapid recurrence [PMID:33805316]. Therapy-induced senescence after temozolomide is triggered by O6-methylguanine damage activating the ATR/ATM-CHK1/CHK2-p53 damage response pathway and does not require activation of the DREAM complex, with p21CIP1 interacting with CDK1 and CDK2 [PMID:40319068]. Temozolomide promotes glioblastoma stemness through senescence-associated reprogramming via HIF1α/HIF2α regulation [PMID:40253386]. Senescent cells remain viable and secrete a large number of factors collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype that paradoxically have pro-tumorigenic effects [PMID:37458855]. Radiation-induced pericyte senescence contributes to blood-brain barrier dysfunction, radiation brain injury, cognitive decline, and glioma cell growth and invasion [PMID:39110121]. Radiation-induced astrocyte senescence promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment in glioblastoma to facilitate tumor regrowth [PMID:38342629]. Whole brain irradiation accelerates brain aging and causes progressive cognitive dysfunction in approximately 50% of surviving patients [PMID:31960269]. Radiation-induced brain injury represents a major challenge for cancer patients undergoing cranial radiotherapy [PMID:39110121]. Senescent astrocytes in irradiated brain can secrete HGF to activate Met in glioma cells and promote migration and invasion [PMID:34580063]. Senescent astrocytes can activate JAK2/STAT3 signaling in GBM cells via IL6 [PMID:41385178]. A multicellular senescent niche including astrocytes, endothelial cells, microglia, and infiltrating immune cells can fuel recurrence [PMID:41749804]. Thus, therapy-induced senescence after radiotherapy and temozolomide is a modifiable determinant of glioblastoma evolution and a therapeutic vulnerability [PMID:41749804].

## Current evidence

In irradiated mouse brains, senescent astrocytes secreted HGF, and the senolytic drug ABT-263 selectively killed senescent astrocytes and significantly attenuated growth of glioma cells implanted in preirradiated brains [PMID:34580063]. Using senolytic agents after radiotherapy to eliminate senescent cells substantially prolonged survival time in preclinical models [PMID:38342629]. Intracranial U251 xenografts in pre-irradiated mice exhibited accelerated tumor growth and reduced survival, phenotypes rescued by the senolytic agent ABT-263 [PMID:41385178]. Navitoclax/ABT263 eliminated senescent cells and reversed whole brain irradiation-induced blood-brain barrier disruption in the mouse brain [PMID:37642933]. Genetic or pharmacological depletion of senescent astrocytes prevented whole brain irradiation-induced impairment of neurovascular coupling responses and protected cognitive function in mice [PMID:31960269]. All-trans retinoic acid eliminated astrocytes that are particularly prone to senescence after radiation, inhibited GBM cell proliferation in vitro, improved survival in GBM-bearing mice, and alleviated radiation-induced cognitive impairment [PMID:39513361]. Clofoctol targeted chemotherapy-induced senescent glioma cells through P53 and triggered apoptotic and ferroptotic death, and synergized with temozolomide to extend survival in a glioblastoma mouse model [PMID:42109835]. The SMAC mimetic birinapant administered as an adjuvant after radiotherapy eliminated senescent GBM cells and prevented the emergence of recurrent tumors in patient-derived xenograft and immunocompetent mouse models [PMID:39972068]. PERK inhibition with GSK2606414 in combination with radiation led to sustained endoplasmic reticulum stress and senescence without SASP, functioned as a senolytic via apoptosis, and prevented recurrence [PMID:39021199]. Navitoclax acted synergistically with irradiation to induce apoptosis in preclinical models of H3K27M-altered diffuse midline glioma [PMID:41430412]. BH3 mimetics targeting BCL-XL reduced metabolic activity and induced mitochondrial apoptosis in senescent pilocytic astrocytoma cells [PMID:35977048]. BMI1 inhibition induced senescence and a senescence-associated secretory phenotype that promoted tumor recurrence, and clearance of senescent cells using BH3 protein mimetics cooperated with BMI1 inhibition to enhance tumor cell killing in vivo [PMID:33086074]. In a phase 2 trial involving 51 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, senolytics combined with anti-PD-1 therapy achieved a 33.3% (95% confidence interval 16.6-54.7%) major pathological response rate with a low incidence of grade 3-4 adverse events at 4.2% [PMID:40855191]. An early phase 1 trial is recruiting patients with previously treated glioma with residual disease to test dasatinib, quercetin, fisetin, temozolomide, LMP744, and autologous TLPO vaccine, with enrollment of 30 and primary outcomes of completion of 3 cycles and turnaround time for scan and marker data [NCT:NCT07025226]. The efficacy of senescence-targeted interventions depends on timing, with early clearance at 1 month after irradiation having no effect on lifespan or functional outcomes, whereas delayed clearance at 4 months reduced frailty, improved neuromuscular and cognitive function, restored blood-brain barrier integrity, improved hepatic metabolic dysfunction, and increased median survival, with the survival benefit most evident in female mice [PMID:42649478]. Brain irradiation induced liver proliferation, increased GFAP levels, and altered ALT and AST activity via mechanisms likely independent of cellular senescence, and these hepatic changes were not reversed by treatment with ABT263 [PMID:41520729]. Elimination of senescent cells with NKG2D CAR-T cells reduced senescent cell burden and suppressed SASP features in an ALS mouse model but did not significantly improve motor function or survival [PMID:41957276]. Temozolomide-induced senescence enhanced sensitivity to a DR5 receptor agonist in p53-proficient, MGMT-deficient U87MG cells but not in p53-mutated, MGMT-proficient T98G cells [PMID:41249587]. In KIAA1549::BRAF-fusion pediatric low-grade glioma models, trametinib inhibited MAPK activity, OIS and SASP signatures, and functionally reduced sensitivity towards senolytic drugs [PMID:40550805]. Glioma-associated senescence is heterogeneous and context-dependent, including phenotypic, functional, spatial, and temporal heterogeneity [PMID:42546852]. Senescence and viral reactivation may fuel glioblastoma progression, including recurrence, suggesting senolytics as a potential strategy but highlighting complexity [PMID:42222436].

## Practice gaps

Clinicians should recognize therapy-induced senescence and SASP as modifiable drivers of glioblastoma recurrence and radiation brain injury and discuss senescence-directed clinical trials, whereas evidence suggests current practice focuses on conventional recurrence and toxicity without senescence-directed stratification [PMID:41749804][PMID:38030881]. Clinicians should consider the timing of senolytic intervention because delayed clearance improved outcomes while early clearance did not, whereas evidence suggests uniform or early senolytic timing may be assumed [PMID:42649478]. Clinicians should select patients using senescence biomarkers and molecular context such as p53/MGMT status, p21, and SASP profiles, whereas evidence suggests senolytic sensitivity is heterogeneous and not yet clinically validated [PMID:41249587][PMID:42222436]. Clinicians should monitor cognitive, blood-brain barrier, and neurovascular effects of radiation-induced senescence and consider senolytic strategies to mitigate them, whereas evidence suggests these sequelae remain underrecognized and lack approved senolytic therapy [PMID:31960269][PMID:37642933]. Clinicians should refer eligible patients with residual glioma to ongoing senolytic combination trials, whereas evidence suggests the only identified glioma senolytic trial is early phase 1 and recruiting [NCT:NCT07025226]. Clinicians should balance efficacy with safety and avoid off-label assumptions, whereas evidence suggests clinical safety data are limited to a phase 2 trial in another tumor type with low grade 3-4 adverse events [PMID:40855191].

## Evidence gaps

Phase 3 randomized data for adjuvant senolytics in glioblastoma are not provided in the SOURCES, which include a phase 2 trial in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and an early phase 1 glioma trial [PMID:40855191][NCT:NCT07025226]. Optimal timing of senolytic administration after radiotherapy and temozolomide in glioblastoma is not established [PMID:42649478]. Predictive biomarkers for senolytic response in glioma are not established [PMID:41249587][PMID:42222436]. Effects of senolytics on cognitive function, blood-brain barrier integrity, and neurovascular coupling in patients are not established [PMID:31960269][PMID:37642933]. Whether senolytic clearance improves survival in human glioblastoma without harming normal brain cells is not established [PMID:39972068][PMID:40855191]. The impact of senescence heterogeneity and escape on senolytic efficacy is not fully delineated [PMID:42546852][PMID:42222436]. Safety of long-term senolytic therapy in cancer survivors and timing-dependent effects require further study [PMID:30737084][PMID:42649478]. Mechanisms of radiation-induced remote organ changes independent of senescence need clarification [PMID:41520729]. Negative or context-dependent results in ALS and pediatric low-grade glioma models need consideration [PMID:41957276][PMID:40550805].

## Proposed learning objectives

1. Identify the mechanisms by which radiotherapy and temozolomide induce senescence in glioblastoma and non-neoplastic brain cells, including SASP, p21, IL-6/JAK2/STAT3, and HGF/Met signaling [PMID:40319068][PMID:41385178][PMID:34580063].

2. Evaluate preclinical and clinical evidence for adjuvant senolytic agents, including ABT-263/navitoclax, all-trans retinoic acid, clofoctol, birinapant, and PERK inhibitors, with attention to efficacy, timing, and safety [PMID:34580063][PMID:39513361][PMID:42109835][PMID:39972068][PMID:39021199][PMID:40855191].

3. Apply evidence on senescence heterogeneity, biomarkers, and trial eligibility to select patients with residual glioma who may be candidates for senolytic clinical trials [PMID:42546852][PMID:41249587][NCT:NCT07025226].

## Assessment questions

1. Which senescence-associated secretory phenotype factor is elevated in irradiated astrocytes and activates JAK2/STAT3 signaling in glioblastoma cells [PMID:41385178]? A. IL6 B. TGF-beta C. VEGF D. PDGF. Correct answer: A. Rationale: Transcriptomic profiling identified IL6 as the predominant SASP factor elevated in irradiated astrocytes, and senescent conditioned medium activated JAK2/STAT3 in GBM cells [PMID:41385178].

2. In the phase 2 trial of senolytics plus anti-PD-1 therapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, what were the reported major pathological response rate and grade 3-4 adverse event rate [PMID:40855191]? A. 33.3% and 4.2% B. 16.6% and 33.3% C. 54.7% and 4.2% D. 4.2% and 33.3%. Correct answer: A. Rationale: The combination therapy achieved a 33.3% (95% CI 16.6-54.7%) major pathological response rate with a low incidence of grade 3-4 adverse events at 4.2% [PMID:40855191].

3. In the INK-ATTAC mouse study of timing-dependent clearance of p16-positive cells after irradiation, what was observed with early clearance at 1 month [PMID:42649478]? A. No effect on lifespan or functional outcomes B. Markedly reduced frailty C. Improved cognitive function D. Increased median survival. Correct answer: A. Rationale: Early clearance had no effect on lifespan or functional outcomes, whereas delayed clearance reduced frailty and improved multiple functional outcomes [PMID:42649478].
